extracted.intended_audience: jurors in patent infringement trials; patent litigators and judges
extracted.subtask_short: patent jury instructions on invalidity and damages
extracted.subtask_description: Model post-trial jury instructions for assessing patent invalidity (e.g., anticipation, statutory bars, obviousness, inventorship) and for determining patent damages (lost profits, price erosion, reasonable royalties). Intended to guide jurors in applying legal standards and evidentiary burdens in U.S. patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention is not new. For a claim to be invalid as not new (i.e., 'anticipated'), all of its requirements must have existed in a single prior art reference that predates the effective filing date (or the date of invention, as applicable). The alleged infringer must prove anticipation by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description in the written reference need not use the same words as the claim, but all claim requirements must be present—stated or necessarily implied—so that a person of ordinary skill could make and use the claimed invention from that single reference. Examples of ways to show lack of novelty include: (1) known or used by others in the U.S. before the date of invention (publicly accessible); (2) already patented or described in a printed publication anywhere in the world before the date of invention (a 'printed publication' is accessible to those interested in the field even if difficult to find); (3) already made by someone else in the U.S. before the date of conception (if not abandoned or secret); (4) described in another issued U.S. patent or published U.S. patent application filed earlier; (5) the named inventor learned the invention from someone else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars (one-year bars / timeliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the patent application was not filed within the time required by law (statutory bar). For invalidity by a statutory bar, all claim requirements must have been present in a reference dated more than one year before the patent application's filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ways to show a statutory bar include: (1) the invention was patented or in a printed publication more than one year before filing; (2) the invention was openly used in the U.S. before that date, and that use was not primarily experimental (i.e., not controlled by the inventor for testing); (3) the invention was sold or offered for sale in the U.S. and was 'ready for patenting' (built or described in enabling detail) before the one-year cutoff; (4) the patent holder had obtained a foreign patent based on an application filed at least one year before the U.S. application. For statutory bars, disclosure may be explicit in a single reference, implicitly disclosed to one skilled in the art, or present even if not understood at the time. Note: this section is inapplicable to post-AIA claims (effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the relevant time (e.g., time of invention or effective filing date). The alleged infringer must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination requires consideration of (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the field, and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations). Do not use hindsight; consider only what was known at the relevant time. Existence of each claim element in the prior art does not automatically prove obviousness because inventions often build on prior art building blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors bearing on motivation to combine / obvious-to-try considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether a claimed invention would have been obvious, consider whether there was a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill to combine known elements in the claimed way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant considerations include: (1) whether the claimed invention was merely the predictable result of using prior art elements according to known functions; (2) whether the invention provided an obvious solution to a known problem; (3) whether the prior art teaches or suggests combining the claimed elements; (4) whether the prior art teaches away from the combination; (5) whether it would have been 'obvious to try' such combinations (e.g., finite, predictable solutions due to design need or market pressure); and (6) whether the change resulted primarily from design incentives or market forces. There must have been a reasonable expectation of success. 'Obvious to try' alone is insufficient in unpredictable technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate obviousness, determine the scope and content of the prior art that a person of ordinary skill would have known at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art includes items in the same field and prior art from different fields that one of ordinary skill might combine using common sense. If parties stipulate to certain art, use the stipulated art; if they dispute, the jury must determine scope and content from the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what differences, if any, exist between the prior art and the patented invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus solely on differences; the test is whether the invention as a whole would have been obvious in view of all prior art. If all elements are disclosed in separate items, consider whether it would have been obvious to combine them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing obviousness, determine the level of ordinary skill a hypothetical person in the field would have possessed at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all trial evidence including: (1) education and experience levels of inventors and others working in the field; (2) types of problems encountered; (3) prior art solutions; (4) rapidity of innovation in the field; and (5) sophistication of the technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence of non-obviousness (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider objective (secondary) evidence that may indicate nonobviousness of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: commercial success due to the invention's merits (not advertising or market forces); satisfaction of a long-felt need; others tried and failed; simultaneous invention by others; copying by others; contemporaneous changes in related technologies or markets; unexpected results; praise by others in the field; surprise or disbelief by persons having ordinary skill; others sought or obtained rights to the patent; and the inventor proceeded contrary to accepted wisdom. Such evidence can shed light on obviousness or lack thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is invalid if it fails to name all actual inventors and only the actual inventors (proper inventorship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be an inventor, a person must make a significant contribution to the conception of at least one claim. Significance is measured against the scope of the full invention. Merely explaining well-known concepts or carrying out experiments under another's instruction does not confer inventorship. Co-inventors need not work physically together but must have some open line of communication during or approximately at the time of inventive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages – burden of proof and measure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the jury finds infringement of any valid claim, it must determine monetary damages adequate to compensate the patent holder. The patent holder has the burden to prove the amount of damages by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not) and with reasonable certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages should place the patent holder in approximately the financial position it would have been in absent the infringement, but must not be punitive and cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. The patent holder need not prove damages with mathematical precision but must avoid remote or speculative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits – general causation (but-for test)
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover lost profits, the patent holder must show a causal relationship between infringement and its lost profits—i.e., but for the infringement, there is a reasonable probability the patent holder would have earned higher profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof may show that absent the infringement the patent holder would have made some portion of the infringer's sales, sold more functionally related products, sold at higher prices, or incurred lower costs. Lost profits are distinct from reasonable royalties and require stronger proof of actual lost business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits – factors to consider (Panduit factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder is entitled to lost profits only if it proves these elements:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Demand for the patented product/method (shown by significant sales of the patent holder's product or of the infringing product containing the patented features); (2) absence of acceptable, available non-infringing substitutes (or quantification of sales despite substitutes), with suggested factors for availability/unavailability; (3) the patent holder had the manufacturing and marketing capacity to make the infringing sales it seeks as lost profits; (4) the amount of profit the patent holder would have made but for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits – market share method
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent holder would have made some, but not all, of the infringer's sales, lost sales may be shown by proving the patent holder's share of the relevant market (excluding infringing products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First establish the relevant market by determining which products are in that market. Products are in the same market if they are 'sufficiently similar' to compete (not significantly higher priced or significantly different in characteristics). The patent holder may be awarded profits equal to its market share even if noninfringing substitutes existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits – collateral sales
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder may recover lost profits on 'collateral' products it would have sold along with the patented product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover such profits the patent holder must prove (1) it is more likely than not it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement, and (2) the collateral product and the patented product together are analogous to components of a single assembly, parts of a complete machine, or constitute a functional unit. Exclude recovery for items with no functional relationship sold only for convenience or business advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits – price erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder can recover damages for price erosion if it proves that, but for the infringement, it would have charged higher prices for some products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award the difference between profits at the higher (but-for) price and actual profits at the lower price. When calculating total losses from price erosion, account for any drop in sales that would have resulted from higher prices. You may also award increased costs (e.g., marketing costs) caused by competition from the infringing product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty – entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent holder has not proved lost profits for all infringing sales, it is entitled to a reasonable royalty for the remaining infringing sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable royalty is the minimum recovery; if lost profits are not fully proven, a reasonable royalty compensates for unauthorized use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty – definition, apportionment, and calculation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the payment that would have resulted from a hypothetical negotiation between the patent holder and the infringer just prior to the start of infringement, assuming both parties acted reasonably and believed the patent was valid and infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate either an ongoing royalty (base revenue times rate) or a one-time lump sum. Determine the base (the product or component revenue on which the royalty applies) and the rate (percentage from hypothetical negotiation). If the patent covers only part of a product, apportion the base to the value of the patented feature; however, if the patented feature is the reason customers buy the whole product or substantially creates the product's value, the base could be the whole product. The patent holder bears the burden to demonstrate the value attributable to the patented component. The ultimate royalty must reflect only the value attributable to the patented features and no more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty – relevant factors (Georgia‑Pacific factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty, consider all facts known and available to the parties at the time infringement began. The instructions list illustrative factors to guide the hypothetical negotiation analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include (as illustrative examples): (1) royalties the patent holder received for licensing the patent; (2) rates the infringer paid for comparable patents; (3) nature and scope of the license (exclusive/nonexclusive, restrictions); (4) patent holder's licensing policy and marketing program to preserve monopoly; (5) commercial relationship between parties; (6) effect of patented specialty in promoting sales of other products (convoyed sales); (7) duration of the patent and license term; (8) established profitability, commercial success, and popularity of the product; (9) utility and advantages over old modes/devices; (10) nature and character of the commercial embodiment and benefits to users; (11) extent of infringer's use and probative evidence of that value; (12) customary portion of profit or selling price in the business for use of the invention; (13) portion of realizable profits attributable to the invention as distinguished from nonpatented elements, manufacturing process, business risks, or infringer-added improvements; (14) opinion and testimony of qualified experts. These factors are nonexclusive and should be weighed according to the evidence.
